utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, let's call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, since the Registrar's microphone was not activated, the case has been called according to the regulations. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can follow in the language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner briefly today. Nicholas Koumjian assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Milan Trbojevic and I'm attorney at law. Together with me is the lead counsel, Mr. John Ackerman, and our assistant, Marela Jevtovic, and our colleague Brian Roberts, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you all. So I understand from what I have been told that we are for the time being suspending Colonel Selak's testimony to enable us to deal with the other witness and ensure his return this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. Colonel Selak was contacted by VWS and asked if he had any objection, and he did not, so therefore we are going to hear the -- Mr. Mujadzic now, and I would very much hope that he could be concluded this afternoon. Mr. Koumjian, who will be calling him, anticipates between an hour and a hour and a half and in lights of the extensive cross-examination he's already had, we would hope that Mr. Trbojevic, as he indicated, would be no more than an hour and a half. One final matter before I leave if I may because I have other matters to deal with this afternoon. Your Honours may recall at some -- about a week or so ago when we just started, Mr. Ackerman raised the question of the timetable and whether there was going to be any break. Your Honours, we have actually discussed the matter. It may be that we've agreed but I don't -- I wouldn't like to speak for Mr. Ackerman, that up until Easter we continue without any breaks as the schedule indicates. Mr. Ackerman, I know, perhaps would like the Easter -- the rest of the Easter week off, if you see what I mean, but we are due back on the Tuesday after Easter at present. Your Honours, my view is very much that I still want to crack on, but I think it's a matter for Your Honours to sort out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Easter is on the 20th, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. Good Friday is the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is being suggested is?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman -- but I don't know we have only discussed it very briefly this morning, this afternoon, rather. But, Your Honour, the only reason I'm raising it and would ask for a decision sooner rather than later is for witnesses. If there is going to be any breaks between now and Easter we certainly need to know and clearly, because we are being asked by the VWS for witnesses to be notified well in advance now. So we need to know if there are to be any breaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour there is no kind of an agreement. We have had a discussion and even though major efforts have been made by judges and other high officials in this Tribunal, we still are never given the Court calendar, so we never know exactly what's going on. I have asked this morning to be furnished with a court calendar. I really don't want to make any representations regarding my feelings about breaks until I have a chance to consult that but one of the things I did discuss with Ms. Korner is going through straight to the Easter break and then making it a longer-than-scheduled break, but we will just have to wait until I look at the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, we will discuss this further. If you want, I can give you my schedule, which is the latest one, updated as on the 17th of January. I can let you have this and you can work on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm fairly certain, Your Honour, that I'll have one when I get back to my flat today. I think it will have been e-mailed to me. I think Mr. Wastelain is quite good about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you do encounter problems, Mr. Ackerman, do let me know, and I will accommodate you. Ms. Korner, if you need to go, please, you're excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, this witness does not enjoy any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's bring him in. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words that you are receiving proper interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal once more. I know that you have given evidence previously in other trials, and therefore I don't need to brief you on the procedure because I suppose that you know it. The usher who is standing right next to you, to your right, will be handing you the text of a solemn declaration. It is tantamount to an oath. It will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal this in the course of your testimony you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So please go ahead with making that solemn declaration by reading that text aloud. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. And you are now going to be examined by Mr. Koumjian, whom you know, I would assume. It's not expected to be a long examination-in-chief because we have the transcripts of your testimony in the other trials. Following the examination-in-chief, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Milan Trbojevic, who is co-counsel with lead counsel, John Ackerman, for the accused in this trial, that is Radoslav Brdjanin. Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The Prosecution would tender Dr. Mujadzic's testimony in the Stakic case. May that transcript be marked as the next exhibit? We would have it as P1601. And the limited redactions have been agreed with the Defence. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is so admitted, P1061.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, just to remind you I know you understand English well. Please pause for the interpretation and make sure, in fact give a second or two after the interpretation is completed before you begin your response so that there is no overlapping of the interpretation with my question. Doctor, you testified in the Stakic case that were you a medical doctor before the conflict in 1992. During the conflict, once you escaped from the Autonomous Region of Krajina territory to Bihac and later to other parts of Bosnia, and after the conflict, up until the time that you testified in the Stakic case. Do you continue to practise medicine? Is that still your profession?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I never stopped exercising my profession, that of a medical doctor. I started working as a physician in 1987 when I obtained a degree from a medical school up until present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that in 1997, were you made the President of the SDA party in Prijedor municipality, at the age of 27. Can you tell the Court what positions first that you held in your party during the conflict from 1991 -- let's say from 1990 until the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise but I think that there has been a mistake in the transcript. We read the year 1997. Actually it was in 1996. I don't know whether this is important for this trial. It is just a minor correction. It is true that in 1990, in the month of August, I was elected president of the municipal board of the Prijedor SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within your party, did you hold any positions at the republican level on the main board and did you represent your party in any -- with -- in front of foreign conferences or delegations of parties from other countries?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, from 1990 when I was elected a republican deputy to the council of citizens -- Chamber of citizens in the BH parliament, at the elections, and in November, 1990, I was elected a member of the main board of the party and in that capacity, together with another deputy, I went to Malta in 1996 to attend a conference of the Christian democrats of Europe. Our party was invited by Mr. Kohl to attend this conference because he thought that our programme, the programme of our party, and its activities, were in accordance with the programme of other Christian democrats in Europe. And in my capacity of a parliament deputy, I attended several conferences in Poland, Romania, and Italy, mainly conferences organised which the OSCE and the parliamentary union.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the SDA party, was there ever an organisation on the regional level, in other words the Banja Luka region, covering the Bosnian Krajina region, and if so, did you hold any position at that regional level?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: We had a regional organisation whose main task was coordination, and since the city of Prijedor had a Bosniak majority, our party won the elections and Prijedor was the only town in the Bosnian Krajina where SDA won the election. So it was decided that the Prijedor should act as some sort of coordination centre, and I was elected president of the regional board of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that we are completely accurate, when you say the SDA won the election in the Prijedor municipality, is it correct, as you testified previously, that the SDA had the most seats of any party in that municipality, not necessarily that they had more than half the seats but they were the leading party in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your explanation is correct. We did not have the 50 -- over 50 per cent majority. We had the most seats in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you -- you testified that you were elected to the parliament. Can you briefly explain how the parliament of Bosnia was divided, what it consisted of, how many houses and the relationship between those two chambers.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time consisted of two chambers, the Chamber of citizens and the Chamber of municipalities. The Chamber of citizens consisted of 130 deputies and the Chamber of municipalities 110. The sessions depended on the competences of the chambers, of course. They were held separately and in respect of laws which required, and that was the case of more than 75 or 80 per cent of laws, which required both chambers, then the sessions would be held jointly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now show you a brief video - it's only about one minute long - of a session of the parliament and ask you, please view it and tell us afterwards whether you were present when this occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an excerpt of a previously marked exhibit -- excuse me, it's a new exhibit, in this case. So it should receive a new number, P -- it actually was part of the Stakic transcripts, so may that be marked P1601-S117? And if that could now be played. It will appear on the monitor in front of you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I'm reading you well - correct me if I'm wrong - Mr. Koumjian, we are talking of excerpts, "The death of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If the booth is ready, if we could play that video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that very brief, obviously less than one minute videotape, do you recall that occurring in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, the video, neither the video nor any translation of it ever showed up on this side of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean? Your monitor was not functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We couldn't see any video, and we didn't hear any translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you -- translation, you didn't need to because there was the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to see it again --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Never mind, never mind. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you describe what it felt like to be present when that speech was given?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Although I heard the speech after this session on several occasions in the media, and also the last time during my testimony in the Stakic case, and I just heard it once again. I always have the same feeling, which is almost identical to the one that I experienced then and there during the session. All members of the parliament, all deputies, including of course myself, after Mr. Karadzic had pronounced this speech, had said those words, we felt fear. We were afraid because the threat seemed to be very serious, and it was expressed with such a tone that we understood it as threatening and we took it very seriously. These words leave me with an even stronger impression nowadays, because his words have almost come true. These things have almost happened. It is true that Bosnia has not disappeared and that Bosniaks, Muslims, have not been exterminated. However, what Mr. Karadzic said was taken seriously and there were serious attempts to implement what he was saying at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come back to the situation that you were in at the time you heard that speech. I want to move on now to talk about Radoslav Brdjanin. Did you know Mr. Brdjanin from the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, both as a deputy and as a colleague, coming from the same region, from the same area that I was from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the same Chamber as Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was in the Chamber of citizens and Mr. Brdjanin was in the Chamber of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe a few moments ago you testified about the percentage of times that the two chambers sat together. Do you mean that they physically sat in the same hall?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. In the building of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were several halls, but there was one big one for so-called general assembly meetings, when both chambers sat together, and when Members of Parliament of both chambers would be together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would there ever come occasions when outside of the hours that the assembly was actually in session, during breaks, there would be social contact or conversation among deputies?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. During the breaks, during parliament sittings, we would meet in the lobby, converse, and discuss laws or current political affairs. But also very frequently we would have quite unofficial conversations to reduce the tensions in parliament and through personal contacts, to try, through personal social contacts, to create a better atmosphere in parliament, which very frequently was not quite what it should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that Mr. Brdjanin was a fellow member of the parliament and that he came from the same region. Can you explain to the Chamber how much contact you had with him as opposed to other deputies, and whether any of those contacts sticks in your memory?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, I never personally officially met with Mr. Brdjanin, and even unofficially we didn't have contacts frequently. Actually, we did meet -- no, not really meet, but during the breaks, the deputies may form groups of five, six, or ten men, and then one might join one group or another, and various subjects were discussed, various political issues that were of current interest at the time. And on one occasion, I joined a group among whom Mr. Brdjanin was, discussing with the other deputies a very important issue at the time. I think, but I'm not quite sure, I don't remember the exact time but I think it could have been in October or November 1991 when there was a discussion on the possibilities of creating Serbian municipalities within Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Mr. Brdjanin was explaining that it would be best for all round if the number of inhabitants of a particular nation in each area were to be gathered together, concentrated, and that that would be the best solution. For instance, that in the Banja Luka region it would be best the number of non-Serbs to be reduced to 2 to 3 per cent of the total and that the best way to do that would be by humane resettlement, for people simply to move out of those areas. Ideas of this kind, one must say, were not advocated only by Mr. Brdjanin. There were other deputies who advocated similar ideas. These ideas, I must admit, were never officially presented at parliament hearings. But I think in contacts between parties, similar -- such ideas were aired and members of my party, and I think other parliamentary parties never embraced such an idea, the one that I have just tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without discussing the substance, did you also have occasions to hear Mr. Brdjanin speak officially in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brdjanin would, with relative frequency, take the floor, and discuss various issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of parliament, as the SDA leader from Prijedor and having a leadership role in the region of Banja Luka, did you frequently have contact with SDS officials, aside from Mr. Brdjanin, other officials in the parliament and the region?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did have several opportunities to talk with Mr. Kupresanin and with Mr. Grahovac, though Mr. Kupresanin was, for a time, the President of the parliament of the autonomous region, before that appointment I had several contacts with him, and I could say that Kupresanin too was a follower of SDS policies, but it should be emphasised that all the people in the SDS were not the same. I shall try to explain, a substantive difference between, for instance, Mr. Kupresanin and Mr. Brdjanin. Mr. Kupresanin, when conducting a discussion, would treat the Bosniak side on an equal footing and he was a person with whom it was possible to negotiate, and reach agreements, and who would give thought to various modalities of coexistence so that he did leave open the possibility of coexistence between Bosniaks and Serbs so that would be the substance of his official position up to a certain period. Whether later on he changed or not, I don't know, but I do know that I never heard Mr. Kupresanin, as far as I know, having changed substantively or deviated from this position. Unlike him, Mr. Brdjanin never even tried to talk to me or anyone else at the level of the region, because he really didn't want to treat us as partners, and he arrogantly rejected any possibility of a discussion. And on a number of occasions, on the media, he made it quite clear, by characterising his statement quite publicly - and when I say "statement," I'm referring to what he said in the assembly - to the effect that the autonomous region or later the area of Republika Srpska should have a small percentage of Bosniaks, 2 to 3 per cent only, and he also made some other derogatory comments about Bosniaks, which now I cannot recollect, but I do know that they were derogatory statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown P1602 and right after that, P1603. Excuse me, they are not marked yet. These are new. The first has -- bears the ERN number in English of 03066843, and in B/C/S of 01816880. It's a memo from Mr. Halilovic. Could that be marked P1602? Perhaps we could put the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I know you read English. If you need to look at the B/C/S, please indicate that. Doctor, in your testimony in the Stakic case, you indicated that after the attack on Hambarine, you were living in a hole for many days - I don't recall now the exact number of days - and eventually along with a couple of other individuals, you made your way on a long journey through villages to Bihac, crossing the river. One of your colleagues was killed trying to cross that river, and in that way, made your way out of the territory controlled by the authorities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The exhibit in front of you, 1602, is it correct that you had not seen this until I showed it to you this weekend?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. I saw it for the first time when you showed it to me here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The memo, which I'm not going to read, it speaks for itself, indicates that there was concern by Mr. Halilovic that you had collaborated with Chetniks. Since your escape from the Autonomous Region of Krajina have you faced allegations from some Bosniaks that you had collaborated or that you had cooperated with the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some people were convinced that the area of Prijedor could have been defended. This was believed by some Bosniaks who were not fully informed of the overall situation in political and military terms. Furthermore, there was a meeting with Mr. Arsic prior -- immediately prior to the takeover of power by the army, that is the SDS in Prijedor, and some people used that as a reason to suspect me of cooperating with the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also face accusations from some Bosniaks -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May the next exhibit be shown? And that would be a report from the security service from Banja Luka, English ERN number in draft is L0036911 to 13, 6911 up to 6913, and the B/C/S ERN number is P0002533 to 2534. May that be marked P1603?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Doctor, would it be correct that you had not seen this document until I showed it to you this weekend?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I hadn't seen the document until you showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that this appears to be a report from the state security department of Banja Luka indicating or accusing you of having been illegally transferred to territory controlled by Muslim authorities, and if we look at -- looking at the last page on the English, page 3, you were described, in addition to describing your grade point average as being 9.7, as an extreme -- as "extreme and wilful in his political and religious convictions." And along with other members of your family in this document, you were described as a type of extremist, an extremist member of the SDA. Did you face similar accusations from Serbian media regarding accusations that you were an extremist who was planning war against the Serbs in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of accusations launched through the Serb media that I, together with a number of other men, had planned to kill a large number of Serbs within the territory of Prijedor municipality and beyond it, and that we had planned various other atrocities against the Serbs, so that in the media, both the printed media and others, there were many articles and broadcasts to this effect, which resulted in a warrant being issued for me and the whole region was looking for me. Mr. Zupljanin personally was committed to arresting me, and so the mass media reported virtually daily as to whether I had been captured or was about to be captured and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I have a document from the Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper from Prijedor dated the 28th of May, 1993, and I repeat, 1993, entitled, "What our sovereign neighbours planned for us." May that be marked next in order which I believe is P1604? And may it be shown to the witness? I'd ask the usher to put the -- if possible, to put the article on the ELMO in a way that the two sets of four photographs can be shown. If we could zoom out, please, a little bit -- move it up a little bit so all the photographs of the eight individuals are shown? Just up another inch would be great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, the article is translated, so I'm not going to go into the details of what it says. But is it correct that the photograph -- that the article and the photographs link eight Bosniaks into two groups, and that four of the individuals, the lower four, to the left, are listed as persons in favour of the war and implementations of instructions from Sarajevo at all costs? Is it correct that that is your photograph on the left of our screens, at the -- in the lower set of photographs, among those individuals in favour of war and the implementation of instructions from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first picture in the bottom row of photographs is mine, the first on the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the individuals in the upper group of four photographs, how they are characterised in the article or the caption?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The upper group of photographs includes that of Mr. Cehajic, Mr. Crnalic, Nedzad Seric, and Camil Pezo. They were described as a group of intellectuals, Mr. Cehajic was also president of the municipality of Prijedor. Mr. Seric was a Judge, the President of the court. As people who also wanted a sovereign Bosnia, but to be achieved in a more peaceful manner and they were described as the more peace-loving current, but the ultimate objectives being identical to those in the bottom group, that is to have a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the bottom group, of which I was said to be one, was described as an extreme group which wanted to achieve those aims by war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of professor Cehajic and the other three individuals, Mr. Seric, Mr. Pezo and the other individual at the top, those listed as being in favour of the peaceful option?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: They are all Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you find a very sad irony in these -- this grouping of eight individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The very sad irony of it is that these people who are described as peace makers, people who wanted to achieve their aims by peaceful means, are all dead, and when this article was written, all these people had already been killed in a brutal manner in the Omarska camp. The men described as extremists in the bottom group as people who wanted war were still alive and free in those days, so I think this is a very blatant distinction which is very obvious at first glance. Those who are dead are for peace and those who are alive were for war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Doctor, we've learned that you are accused by the Serbian SDS authorities of being a terrorist planning war, and that you were suspected by some of your fellow Bosniaks as being a collaborator. Can you tell the Chamber what the actual situation was and explain your actions at that time. Did you plan a military attack in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: To plan a military attack on Prijedor would be something quite illogical and senseless because we didn't have a chance, in view of what we had in our possession. We didn't have a chance of keeping or defending Prijedor. In fact, we never planned any attack. All that we had planned was defence in the case of an attack, which was obvious and quite evident that it would come, judging by the previous situation that we had all seen in Croatia, also judging by the threats made by Mr. Karadzic, the threats made by Mr. Brdjanin, and many other members of the SDS, judging by the testimony of our own recruits who had witnessed with their own eyes on the battle front in Novska in Croatia that a number of soldiers in the Yugoslav People's Army at the time were wearing Chetnik insignia and committing terrible atrocities in Croatia. And it was only logical for us to expect, once the army withdrew from Croatia, that a similar attack - and also bearing in mind political develop developments - that such an attack would be launched against us as well. That is why certain measures were taken in the sense of defence from a possible attack. Also, as far of -- as the doubts expressed by the Bosniaks, or rather the suspicion that is were made by the Bosniaks were done because they were not fully aware of the balance of forces. Both in the municipality and the region as a whole. The Banja Luka Corps --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you're about to answer my next question. Can you describe the balance of forces and -- you testified that you were a medical doctor rather than a military man, whether your information, or whether you consulted with other persons of military background regarding the possibility of defending Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I do wish to point out that I'm a medical doctor and I never had anything to do with military organisation. I was not a member of the army. I don't have any inclination or talent for military affairs, and I never made any attempts to do so. But of course as a person who was a member of parliament from the area at the time, and a local political leader, I was informed of the situation as it developed. And I also had certain contacts with Mr. Halilovic who came to Prijedor on two occasions, and who actually formed the Patriotic League for Bosnia-Herzegovina, the aim of which was to carry out certain defensive preparations which would preserve the integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Patriotic League itself was constructed on the basis of the platform of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So as an organisation, it wasn't intended only for Bosniaks. Its programme envisaged that it would be open to all those who wanted to defend Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Halilovic tell you regarding the possibility of defending the Prijedor region and the Banja Luka region from the forces of the former JNA and the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: On the basis of their military assessments, it was indicated that unfortunately they stood no chances, that it was impossible to successfully defend the overall area of Banja Luka. I had had some information prior to that. I mean I knew that the Banja Luka Corps was one of the most strongest -- one of the strongest corps in the former JNA, and that it had a large number of armour vehicles, helicopters, artillery pieces, different artillery pieces, and that the area of Prijedor could be easily accessed by tanks, because it was located in a valley, in a plain, and that we could not defend it. The republic board of the Patriotic League said that it was perhaps possible to defend the left bank of the Sana River which excluded some parts of the municipalities of Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc, and the area was actually directly linked thereby to the Bihac area located behind but also on the banks of the Sana. So it was necessary for the Territorial Defence from the Bihac area to provide assistance to the TO units in our area, and that they tried together to defend the left bank of the Sana. That was assessed to be the only reasonable solution, that that was the only plan that could be implemented realistically speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you discussed in your previous testimony that this plan became impossible once -- correct me if I'm wrong -- Bosanska Krupa fell to the SDS forces. Is that correct? I may have the wrong municipality.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. The plan was to establish a corridor towards Bosanska Krupa and unfortunately on the 23rd of April, Bosanska Krupa was attacked in a very swift military attack by JNA. It was taken possession of, and all communications with the area of Bihac were thus severed. Therefore, the area of Banja Luka remained isolated and encircled from all sides. This rendered this last possibility to defend the left bank of the Sana no longer viable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given this military situation, can you tell us if at any time either before the SDS takeover of the elected government of Professor Cehajic on the 30th of April, or after that, up to the attacks on Hambarine and Kozarac, was there in Prijedor any plans for an offensive against the JNA, against the Serbian party or Serbian citizens in Prijedor? What was your attitude towards conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As I have already indicated, all our plans were of a defensive nature. We never had a single plan which would have implied an attack by any unit, attack on any Serb settlement or like. As I said, all our plans were defensive plans, plans to defend. We never planned any attack whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned today your meeting with Colonel Arsic which you described in your testimony in the Stakic case, and I believe you also in your Stakic testimony, you described a meeting in the police station earlier that day. During that meeting, did a telegram arrive? Or was there some indication that a telegram --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of April, 1992, after several requests of the Autonomous Region of Krajina to have Prijedor annexed to the Autonomous Region of Krajina and to have the Prijedor police station placed under the control of the Banja Luka public security station, we held a meeting with political representatives from both the municipality and other political parties, together with employees of the police. The meeting was held in the police building. We tried to maintain a status quo, and we informed the representatives of the police that it was better to continue having contact with Sarajevo, that it was from there that their salaries were coming and that the region still had no -- its own resources, so that this communication was necessary. And in case of any problems, we thought, we said that we could sit down and try to solve them together, in order to avoid any possible conflict. Almost at the very -- at the end of the meeting, all of a sudden, Milos Jankovic appeared. He's the communications chief with the public security station in Prijedor. He was very hysterical. He waved a document. He held it in his hand, and he said, "You see what they want? You see what Alija Delimustafic and others from Sarajevo want? They want us to attack our JNA. See for yourself. This is what they want. This is what they request for [as interpreted] us. And they want us to be loyal to them." I asked Mr. Jankovic to show us the document, to tell us what this was all about, which is not what he wanted, and he simply said that the document had arrived directly from the minister and that he could not give it to us. However, on the same day, at 5.00 p.m., Colonel Arsic wanted me to come to the barracks as soon as possible, and I asked him for this meeting to be organised at a neutral location because I was already afraid that I could be arrested by the military, because of the situation which was getting increasingly tense, I felt uncomfortable. However, Colonel Arsic insisted and he said, "Please come here as soon as possible. It is very important. Mr. Miskovic is chairing the meeting and we have to get together as soon as possible." So after he insisted, I went to the barracks and Colonel Arsic showed me a document. As soon as I got in, he threw it at me and he said, "Mujadzic, what do you make of this? What do you think about this".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 22 line 16 there is a sentence that says, "This is what they request for us," and actually what it should say is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: From us, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I know there are many more important details about that meeting but they are contained in your Stakic transcript, so I'm not going to go through all of those now. What I'd now like to do is have that telegram placed on the ELMO, and that's P1167. While it's being prepared, let me just ask you, you mentioned Simo Miskovic, is it correct he was the President of the SDS party in Prijedor at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He was the president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you talked about Milos Jankovic as the head of the communications department in the police station. Do you know of his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb by ethnicity. I mean he still is. He's alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned Mr. Delimustafic. Is it correct that he was a Bosniak and was the Minister of the Interior at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He's a Bosniak and Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the meeting with Arsic, did Mr. Arsic finally show you the telegram in question?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He showed me the document, and wanted me to provide an explanation of the document, and also to express our attitude towards the document and tell him how it is that we intend to react to the issues raised by the document, what our response would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the English could be put on the ELMO and the witness be given the B/C/S. This is obviously a photocopy of the original that you have with some handwriting dated the 11th of May, but the document in type bears the date 29 April, 1992. Is this -- does this appear to be the same -- a copy of the same document that Colonel Arsic showed you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a copy of the document shown to me by Mr. Arsic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document indicates that its pursuant to an order of the Presidency. Can you tell us what was the reaction of the Presidency to this document, the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior, Mr. Alija Delimustafic, with this document and on the basis -- on an order issued by the Presidency of BH, to issue further orders to all police stations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to set up road barricades and lay siege to all military garrisons and try to sever all communications of these garrisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I stopped you. Thank you for following my hand signal -- because perhaps my question wasn't clear. Did the Presidency react to this document after it became public? Was there an acknowledgment or a denial of the authenticity of this document by the Presidency of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The Presidency stated their position on the following day regarding this document. They declared that the document was not authentic and that it had never issued any such order or instruction to the Minister of the Interior. In other words, the presidency denied the authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Minister of the Interior, the supposed author, Mr. Delimustafic? Did he admit or deny this document being a genuine document, order that he had sent?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I think that in the press release, that is what was said on behalf of the Presidency, said that the Presidency had not reached such a decision and that the Ministry of the Interior, of course, could not issue a document of this nature, thereby denying the possibility on the part of the Ministry of the Interior to have sent out a document of this kind, because obviously if the Presidency had not reached a decision to that effect then the Minister of the Interior had no authority to issue a document like this either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the addressees of this telegram, it indicates to chief, all security services centres, and I believe they would also be known as CSBs. Would it be correct, then, that this document would have been sent according to the addressees to persons such as Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, the head of the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You can see from the title that the document was supposed to be sent, that it was sent to all chiefs of public security stations, and the MUPs, the public security stations in the city of Sarajevo itself, which means that Mr. Zupljanin must have received this document too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that in Prijedor, on -- in your Stakic testimony, the police chief was Mr. Talundzic, a Bosniak, and you also told us today that head of the communications department that received the telegram was Mr. Jankovic, a Serb. Just within the Krajina region, if you recall now, how many of the public security stations had Serb chiefs of police?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: At the security services centre in Banja Luka, there were several public security stations, 17, that is, except in Jajce, whose population was Croatian and Bosniak by majority more than 86 per cent. And Jajce was actually part of central Bosnia, not the Prijedor Krajina. Prijedor was the only municipality in which the security services centre, the public security station was headed by a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question that I mean to ask you before I leave and before I forget it, very simple: How long does it take to drive from the centre of Prijedor to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: From the centre of Prijedor to the centre of Banja Luka, if you drive normally, at an average speed, between 90 and 100 kilometres per hour, I think you need 45 minutes. It's about 58 kilometres, a little more than 30 miles. Prijedor and Banja Luka are very close, as cities, which was damaging for the development of Prijedor, because Banja Luka was the regional centre and it somehow stunt Prijedor in its economical growth because towns such as Bihac, Brcko, and Doboj had this regional character, although they were significantly smaller than Prijedor. I use this example only to illustrate to you the vicinity of Prijedor to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just in the interests of time I want to move on. The fourth paragraph of this document calls on -- indicates, orders, "The planning and launching of combat activities throughout the territory of the Republic of BH is to be accelerated." What effect do you think this order would have upon Serbian police officers and Serbian citizens in places like Prijedor? What effect do you think this would have upon their attitude towards their Muslim and Croat neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't fully understand your question. Would you be so kind and repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fourth paragraph of the telegram orders "The planning and launching of combat activities throughout the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is to be accelerated." Do you think that this document, if taken by Serbs as genuine, would have an effect upon Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: By all means. If this document were accepted as an authentic document, and I believe that the majority -- well, I'm actually not sure whether anyone knew that this document was not an authentic document sent by the Ministry of the Interior. Most of the people really believed that this document was authentic, and since they believed in its authenticity, they thought that it was necessary to undertake some emergency action as countermeasure, because according to this document, Bosniaks, Muslims, were preparing an attack against the army, which in the view of the majority of the Serbs, constituted an attack on themselves, against themselves. This document served as a justification for the army and the SDS to organise a putsch in Prijedor which took place only a day later, after the arrival of this document, on the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you've already commented upon the reality of the military situation, so I won't ask you about how logical paragraph 4 is. But the first three paragraphs of this order concern -- are orders to block the JNA from pulling out of Bosnia. Doctor, which political parties in Bosnia on the 29th of April, 1992, opposed the JNA pulling out its equipment and men from Bosnia and which parties were in favour of the JNA leaving Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: All political parties, including the SDA, and with the exception of SDS, were in favour of the JNA pulling out from Bosnia and Herzegovina. There had already been many such attempts, politically speaking, but the SDS refused this emphatically and they insisted that the JNA should remain in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So in addition to the already-stationed units in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the units that had withdrawn from Croatia arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was in this way turned into a large military warehouse, the territory with the very strong concentration of the former JNA, its personnel. So everybody with the exception of the SDS was in favour of the JNA pulling out from Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, with the insistence of the SDS, the JNA remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this is why this document in itself is not logical. On one hand, that all parties, including the SDS, should request that the JNA leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on the other hand, this document requests the JNA to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it is contradictory. It's not logical. Not to speak of the fact that the document of this kind was sent to a place such as Prijedor, whose chief of communications department is a Serb, and so they would have known that the document would have ended in the hands of a Serb. I mean, there is a number of illogical things about this document, which can point to the fact that it is not an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your Stakic testimony, you go on to describe the overthrow of the elected government the next day in Prijedor. And I want to move on then to just another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May the witness be shown, the Kozarski Vjesnik of the 28th of June, 1992, and the English translation has the number L0088624. I don't know if Your Honour wants to take the break now before I go into this? It actually might be helpful because I may have another document translated by the time we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's perfectly okay with us, Mr. Koumjian. This document will be P1605?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: 5, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And just to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The translation deals with the article in the lower left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The previous document, the telegram that we have been discussing, is included in the binder that was handed to us as D6A and B, but I took it that it has already been exhibited in this case as P1617 or something like that, so it's not being tendered again, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, correct. It's P1167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1167, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: According to Ms. Gustin who is never wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 15-minute break and we'll continue after that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Koumjian. You were about to start dealing with Exhibit P1605, which has just been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. I see on the ELMO we have the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, in your testimony in Stakic, you referred to a friend of yours, a Dr. Zeljko Sikura, who you indicated was of Czech ethnicity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the religion of Dr. Sikura was.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sikura was a Catholic, of Catholic faith, though he never spoke of his religion, nor did he give the impression of being a particularly religious man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, among the most extreme elements of Serbian nationalists, would Dr. Sikura be characterised, together with any other ethnic group, being a Czech Catholic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: No. He was actually described as an Ustasha, like all other Croats that were considered to be extremists. So Dr. Sikura was described in this way, probably only because he was of Catholic faith, but in the media, he was also referred to as the Monster Doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Sikura is not actually named in this article entitled "Monster Doctor." Can you tell us why you believe it refers to Dr. Sikura?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Because in Prijedor, it was made public that Dr. Sikura had planned to sterilise Serb children, to carry out abortions without any reason for Serb women, expectant women, though he was newly graduated from medical school and there was no possibility of him being able to do any such thing. But knowing Mr. Sikura's personality, as he was a colleague of mine and he worked with me in the same outpatient's clinic for more than two years, I know that on a number of occasions, or rather very frequently, he went to Serb villages and helped the Serbs, without any remuneration, and actually, he was a person who was beloved, particularly in Tomasica, beloved by Serbs. He was a very popular person among Serbs because he helped them a lot, and that is why this article says a lot. Dr. Sikura was not the only person who paid a high price for being popular among the Serbs and for assisting them. Several other doctors and other intellectuals were victimised for that very reason. Many might wonder how is that possible, that on the one hand, he did so many good things for the Serbs, and on the other side, was described as a monster, somebody who had planned the gravest crimes against the Serbs. The reason is that in the territory of Prijedor municipality, relationships between Bosniaks and Serbs were traditionally good. And Prijedor, as a town, was taken as an example of such good relationships between Bosniaks and Serbs. So the aim of this was to say that if Dr. Sikura who had done so many good deeds, had planned such crimes against you, then you can imagine what others had planned to do to you. So this kind of a propaganda ploy, which climaxed unfortunately with the killing of a number of people, was designed to spread paranoia among citizens of Serb ethnicity to the effect that all Bosniaks and all Croats were planning evil things against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, correct me if I'm wrong, that this morning going through some issues of Kozarski Vjesnik that I had, you found an article that did in fact refer by name to Dr. Sikura and to another doctor, Dr. Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May that be marked next in order, Your Honour? I have a draft translation only available. That would be P1606. If the original could be put on the ELMO? And I'm not sure if the Defence has got a copy yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we don't have a copy as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. We have a revised draft, only one copy that just arrived, and we have an earlier draft that we could hand out but we'll have a final later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, is it correct that this article refers in the -- I believe the first paragraph, to the recent uncovering of Dr. Sikura?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I shall read it out as it is just one sentence. "The recent unmasking of Dr. Sikura, who for years applying monstrous methods worked in a planned manner to reduce the birth rate among the Serb people sheds new light on the professional activities of certain doctors of Prijedor." So it can be seen from this article too that the other article relates to Dr. Sikura, and similar news reports were published in other media so this only confirms what I said a moment ago, that some people paid a high price precisely because they had such -- were on such good terms with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This article also discusses alleged mistreatment by Dr. Osman Mahmuljin of the ill Dr. Dukic. Can you tell us the ethnicity of these two doctors?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mahmuljin was a Bosniak and Dr. Dukic was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a medical doctor and a resident of Prijedor, do you have any comment having read this article of the alleged mistreatment of Dr. Dukic by Dr. Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The article says that allegedly Dr. Mahmuljin administered the wrong therapy to Dr. Dukic and that this could have provoked his death, because Dr. Dukic that day had had an infarction, a heart attack, and that is why Dr. Mahmuljin treated him. Though perhaps that may not be of interest to this Tribunal, I have studied in detail the therapy that was administered to Mr. Dukic, that is what allegedly Dr. Mahmuljin administered to Dr. Dukic, and it is clear that the medicines given, such as Ribokiene [phoen], which is still administered in the United States in the case of a heart attack, Dr. Mahmuljin obviously gave the right therapy, but this article is intended for the public at large, who are untrained and unable to notice the shortcomings and the same was to give another illustration of the fact that all Bosniaks were thinking up evil deeds against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a doctor Esad Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I did. I did know Dr. Sadikovic, who was very popular as a physician and as a person in Prijedor municipality. He's also a person who spoke two or three foreign languages, including English, and for many years he was a member of international medical teams all over the world. I think he went to Samoa and some other countries. He was married to a Serb and he personally considered himself to be a cosmopolitan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Dr. Sadikovic's attitude was towards the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sadikovic, who was by ethnicity a Bosniak, but as I just observed, by his own beliefs he was cosmopolitan and he was on very goods terms with all the citizens of Prijedor, including Serbs of course, and he believed that in those hard times, he could be of assistance in avoiding a potential conflict, which he realised too was inevitable, and that is why he invested a great deal of effort to try and calm the situation, and to bring influence to bear on the Serb side so that the conflict be avoided at all cost. Actually, he spoke simultaneously with the Bosniak and the Serb sides and he sincerely endeavoured to preserve peace and have the conflict avoided. However, Dr. Sadikovic, in the media, was subsequently described as a person who had secret plans and hidden malicious intentions against Serbs, and he could also be placed within the same category as Dr. Sikura and Dr. Mahmuljin, who were also on very good terms with citizens of Serb ethnicity. And unfortunately all three doctors, including Dr. Sadikovic, was killed, precisely because of his peace-making efforts. He was killed brutally in the Omarska camp, as were the other two physicians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I've reached -- I've exceeded the time I wanted to spend so just one additional question: Having been a political leader of the SDA at the time, can you -- looking back now, can you tell us why you believe Prijedor suffered so brutally during 1992 following the takeover of the SDS? Why Prijedor in particular?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is interesting to note that many places in Bosanska Krajina and throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, in which less than 30 per cent of the population were non-Serbs, did not suffer so badly, or rather the citizens of those towns in -- were expelled in a "peaceful manner," in quotation marks, but there were no massacres or many killings, except for individual incidents that did occur within the territories of other municipalities. However, the greater suffering occurred along the Sana River valley where the population percentage-wise were evenly split with the Serbs, and this applies to Sanski Most, to Kljuc, Bosanski Novi, and Prijedor. So that is one of the reasons, however, not -- it is not the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. main reason. Prijedor was known in the former Yugoslavia as a town that was an example of brotherhood and unity and an example of Tito's resistance movement and the songs that were sung on the mountains of Kozara surrounding Prijedor were taken as an illustration of brotherhood and unity of all the peoples of Yugoslavia. And that was also the reason why Ante Markovic the former Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, his campaign for the reformist forces and the unity of the former Yugoslavia, which should have included all the peoples, was launched initially from Prijedor, that is the slopes of Mount Kozara. Dr. Karadzic did not have a great deal of confidence in the SDS leadership in Prijedor, precisely because the SDS had lost the elections, and he believed this to be the reason why what he considered to be poor or bad Serbs lived in Prijedor. And according to Dr. Karadzic, such poor Serbs were all those who accepted coexistence with the Bosniaks. And as Prijedor was known as a town of coexistence, then he wished -- or let me correct myself, the crimes that happened in Prijedor happened precisely because of the design to break or destroy the image of Prijedor as a town of good relationships between Bosniaks and Serbs, as a town that symbolised the brotherhood unity, and that by crimes committed against the Bosniaks, there should be a chasm created between the Serbs and the Muslims, that mutual hatred be instigated which would culminate in the absolute impossibility of joint life by Serbs and Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is why Prijedor, as a symbol of brotherhood and unity, experienced the greatest suffering and the greatest massacres in that period of time in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, it will only be Srebrenica which came later that will surpass this tragic record of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that Dr. Karadzic classified as the bad Serbs those that would accept coexistence with Bosnians. Based upon your experience in the parliament with Mr. Brdjanin, did Mr. Brdjanin fit Dr. Karadzic's category of bad Serbs or was he of the category that Dr. Karadzic preferred?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Even though I heard later that Mr. Brdjanin himself was not on good personal terms with Mr. Karadzic, which was probably due to the rivalry, the traditional rivalry between Banja Luka and Sarajevo, and the bulk of the SDS leadership in those days came from Sarajevo rather than Banja Luka, and Mr. Brdjanin appeared on the scene later on as a very powerful regional leader. However, Mr. Brdjanin clearly, by his statements and behaviour and subsequent activities, is within the group of very good Serbs, according to Karadzic's assessment, and this resulted in a very good career that he made in the SDS, and quickly climbed to the position of the President of the Crisis Staff in Banja Luka. So there is no doubt that Mr. Brdjanin, by his statements and behaviour, belongs to the group of the most loyal followers of the SDS, true to the ideas of Dr. Radovan Karadzic and their very substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Perhaps we could deal later with the admission of the Stakic exhibits or now, as Your Honour prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly that will be more practical, Mr. Koumjian. I thank you. Yes, Doctor, now you're going to be cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic. Mr. Trbojevic, if you prefer to come forward here rather than stay -- it's up to you. I mean -- because I notice that the microphone is in front of your assistant. Yes, okay. Thank you, ma'am. Now, Mr. Trbojevic and Dr. Mujadzic, you both speak the same language. It has been a common occurrence here that the moment he finishes the question, the witness jumps in straight with the answer, not giving a chance to the interpreters to translate into English. So please, Doctor, when he finishes his question, do allow a very short interval of time you start giving your answer, so that you will give time to the interpreters to finish their translation. At the same time, Mr. Trbojevic, I don't need to repeat there to you because you're quite familiar with the problem and you have been very cooperative in the past, although not always. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mujadzic, I'm afraid I have to go back a little. I know that you have given extensive testimony and that you have been also extensively cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the impression somehow that my microphone is being turned off and on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's turned off now. It's turned on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it will be okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is difficult to summarise all your statements and testimonies, there were two such testimonies and two different cross-examinations. However, I should like to begin with the subject of the break-up of Yugoslavia. You addressed the issue for the first time in the Tadic case. I believe you also spoke about it on the 27th of May in the Stakic case, and one could perhaps reach the conclusion that the conflict started with the amendments to the constitution of 1974?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and characterise for me the nature of the conflict that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not referring to the conflict itself. I think that it is beyond dispute that the SDA and SDS had in their programmes, the preservation of Yugoslavia at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That was part of the SDA programme as well, and part of its policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, the constitution of Serbia was amended, autonomous provinces were abolished in this constitution, and from that moment on, the policies of the respective policies of SDS and SDA started to change and become more different. You will remember the adoption of the law on the -- on the tax and the replenishment of the budget for the purposes of the JNA, the federal budget, that is, that that was discussed at one point in time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, also the functioning of the federal institutions. I think you talked about this in the Stakic case, transcript page 3.645. You said that the SDS wanted the continuation of the federal financing of the JNA, that HDZ categorically opposed this, and that SDA found some sort of middle ground by proposing a special fund for this purpose, whose expenses and intention would be determined later on. I think I have more or less correctly paraphrased your words?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. If you have finished your question, I shall take the liberty to be more precise. The change in this constitution took place earlier on. If you remember, these amendments took place at the time prior to the existence of both SDS and SDA. It was during the time of the former League of Communists of Yugoslavia and League of Communists of the Republic of Serbia. So during that period of time, this could not have been a bone of contention between SDS and SDA, since they did not exist at the time. That could not have been the subject of their disagreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question would be as follows: Do you agree that at the time that this was all happening, I am referring to the taxes and the financing coming from the federal institutions, that political positions against the financing, federal financing, of the JNA were designed actually to destroy the existing federation? That that was the objective?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Once again, I have to ask the counsel to be more precise. Whose positions do you have in mind? Whose political positions are you referring to? Which political parties did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I quoted your testimony on page 3.645 when you said that the SDS was in favour of the continuation of the federal financing of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the HDZ was against and the SDA were also --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers be asked to slow down, please? We cannot follow. Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You have not been following the advice that I gave you. You're jumping straight one after the other, and not giving the interpreters a chance to do their job, their work, properly. Mr. Trbojevic, please slow down. And Dr. Mujadzic, please allow an interval before you answer, because you're not allowing even Mr. Trbojevic to finish his question. Any way the position -- let me paraphrase it myself. Correctly, Mr. Trbojevic is reminding you that in -- in reference to your previous testimony, he explained or he paraphrased what was the position taken by the various political parties with regard to the financing of the JNA, saying that the SDS wanted to retain the status quo, the Croat -- Croatian party was definitely against, and your party, the SDA, took a middle road and was not exactly against as much as the Croatian party was. And the question that he is putting to you is whether, in your opinion, the fact that your party and the Croatian party took a different view, approach, to that of the SDS was designed specifically to undermine, to destroy, the federation. Did I interpret your question well, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot assess the intentions of HDZ but I know that by trying to reach a middle ground, the intentions of SDA were to preserve and maintain stability and to find a compromise, a transitional solution, so to speak, and not to create instability or undermine the federation as was suggested by Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These talks took place at the time when Croatia and Slovenia were asking for independence. However, the issue was not yet being discussed -- this issue was not yet mentioned in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 26th of May, 1996, in your first testimony, you said that the SDA policy was at an equal distance from both, from these two other parties, and that this implied an equal distance or an equal closeness both to Serbia and Croatia, with respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is what you stated. This is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... What is your question, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have just paraphrased the testimony of the witness, that is that the SDA believed that Bosnia and Herzegovina should not -- neither remain in Yugoslavia nor leave Yugoslavia, but that on the basis of the theory that they termed equidistance, that they realised or implement an equal distance or maintain an equal distance towards Serbia and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I think my original words should be used as a starting point. If you want me to, I can now answer your question or explain what the issue was all about. The term equidistance, that is the equal distance, was based on the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina consisted of three peoples, Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats, who were two -- who were equal constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that for the stability of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because of this fact, it was necessary for Bosnia and Herzegovina, in its entirety, to have equal relations with Serbia and Croatia. Any decision as to the closer relationship with either Bosnia or Herzegovina [as interpreted] because of the nature of its composition, would end-- would result in a break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So what you have termed as the theory of equidistance was actually the only possible policy not of the SDA but of Bosnia-Herzegovina in its entirety. Both before and after, and even today, the policy of Bosnia and Herzegovina should advocate this position. The objective should be to maintain equally good relationship with Croatia and Serbia, and this is what the term meant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction page 42 line 13, "The closer relationship with either Serbia or Croatia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that that was my understanding too. However, SDS -- this policy implied the remaining in Yugoslavia, and the SDA, through its leadership, entered into certain agreements or treaties with Croatia, both public and secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, we are receiving French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we did too for a while. But I think the situation now is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you heard me. Especially lately some transcripts have been published, transcripts of talks held at Mr. Tudjman's office, that there would be some secret confederations with Croatia and so on and so forth, and it is in this context that I am asking you the following: Was SDA really in favour, for an equal distance with respect of both sides, or was it merely a political game which of course would not be that unusual?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Never before the war, and before the conflict, did any talks take place between the leadership of the SDA and Croatian Democratic Union or President Tudjman for that matter, with respect of the creation of some Croatian-Muslim coalition or Bosnian-Croatian federation. Nor were there any talks ever, any talks that would be targeted against the citizens of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact remains, however, that the activities with the purpose of secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia were taken on the basis of this attitude, the attitudes that were contrary to the wishes of the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: When you say "contrary to the wishes of the Serb people," I don't know exactly what you mean. Could you be more precise, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact is that the Serbian deputies in the parliament clearly declared themselves as opposed to the secession. The fact is also that there was a referendum, a plebiscite actually. How many people turned out is perhaps not very important here; however, it expressed their wish to remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt that the SDS deputies were explicitly in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia. However, the SDS deputies were not representatives of the Serbian people in general, as the deputies of the SDA were not representatives of the Croatian people. They never had an exclusive right to represent one single people. In other words, a single political party cannot act as a representative of a single people except in fascism, because such things happened in those societies. I don't think that this is something that you would characterise in this manner. So I don't think that the SDS represented the Serb people, nor can we say that the HDZ and SDA represented Croatian or Muslim people respectively so this is not something that you can identify with the wishes of the Serbian people in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't trying to suggest that. But today, from this time distance of more than ten years, I think that we have to agree that there was no doubt that the Serbian people wanted to stay in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I've already mentioned in several of my testimonies, that there is no doubt, and that there was no doubt, that the Bosniak people wanted to preserve Yugoslavia and wanted to stay in Yugoslavia. But President Izetbegovic at negotiations that you remember very well - I'm sure, on a number of occasions, through initiatives with the President of Macedonia, Mr. Gligoroff - demonstrated this and endeavoured in every possible way to preserve Yugoslavia in any form. And in doing so, he actually demonstrated that he, or rather we Bosniaks, were most eager to preserve Yugoslavia at all cost, and that is the bare truth. However, it was precisely Mr. Milosevic who did not agree to any of those proposals, but one must say that the Slovene and Croatian presidents didn't either so that it is the Bosniaks who least wanted the disintegration of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I remind both of you, please, that this is not the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where you may have exchanged political blows in the past but a Trial Chamber trying Mr. Brdjanin. So please may I call you to order and restrict yourself to what is strictly relevant to the case.
